SK6021 A type is named like an exception and is not one

The Exception suffix is a promise that catch (SomethingException) will work, and a type that does not derive from System.Exception cannot keep it.

CategoryDesign
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS2166

Why

Exception at the end of a type name is not decoration; it is the one naming convention in .NET that a language construct depends on. A reader who sees PaymentDeclinedException writes catch (PaymentDeclinedException), and if the type does not derive from System.Exception that line does not compile — the name has cost them the time it takes to find out why. Everything else that keys on the suffix is misled the same way: throw, exception filters, logging that unwraps an AggregateException, analyzers that check exception design, and the reviewer skimming a diff. The type is either an exception and should say so in its base list, or it is not one and should not claim the suffix. Neither answer is a mechanical edit, which is why the rule has no fix.

Example

Instead of:

public sealed class PaymentDeclinedException {
    public string Reason { get; init; } = string.Empty;
}

Write:

public sealed class PaymentDeclinedException : Exception {
    public PaymentDeclinedException(string message) : base(message) { }
}

When it does not fire

The suffix, never the substring. ExceptionHandler, ExceptionFilter, ExceptionPolicy, ExceptionDispatcher and ExceptionExtensions are all correctly named and none of them is an exception — and none of them is reported, because each ends in the word that says what it really is. That is the whole of the containment question: a type about exceptions puts Exception in the middle and its own noun at the end, and only a type claiming to be one puts Exception last. Nothing here looks for the substring.

Interfaces are out of scope. An interface cannot derive from System.Exception, so IRetryableException is not a mistake this rule could ask anyone to correct — the finding would have no available answer. enum and delegate declarations are excluded for the same reason. Classes, structs, records and record structs are all reported: a struct named …Exception cannot be one either, but there the name is the thing to change and the message says so.

A type named exactly `Exception` is left alone. It is either System.Exception itself, seen while analysing a framework, or a deliberate shadow whose author already knows; "derive from Exception" is not advice that means anything to a type named Exception.

An unresolved base is silence, not a finding. If any type in the base chain is an error type the rule stops and says nothing, because "does not derive from Exception" and "the compilation could not tell" produce the same answer from a naive walk and only one of them is a finding. This is why the rule is semantic and does not run under --load=loose.

⚠ No fix, deliberately. The two repairs are adding : Exception — which changes what the type is, and drags in the constructors and the serialization surface an exception is expected to have — and renaming, which is a solution-wide edit that Skala's one-file text-edit model cannot make. Guessing between them would be guessing at intent. hasFix: false is the first in the catalogue and is a knowing choice rather than an omission.

The shape that is genuinely borderline is a name ending in the word by accident: ThrowsNoException, AssertsOnException. They are rare, they read badly to a human as well, and they are the case to baseline.
